questions.q: Which of these countries is India's neighbour across the sea but does NOT share a land boundary with India?
questions.a: Sri Lanka: it is an immediate neighbour across the waters, while Nepal, Bhutan and Myanmar share land boundaries with India.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a maritime neighbour, as the chapter explains it?
o: A country joined to another by a shared sea or ocean, even without a land border
A country that shares a land boundary running along a river valley
Any country that lies on the same continent as another country
A country that can send its goods only through another country's ports
questions.a: A country joined to another by a shared sea or ocean, even without a direct land border.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India is described as a maritime nation.
Reason (R): India is surrounded by the sea on three sides.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: being surrounded by the sea on three sides is why India has always been a maritime nation.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Indian Ocean.
I. Half of the world's container ships are transported through it.
II. It is the second-largest ocean in the world.
III. It carries one-half of the world's oil.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I only. Half of the world's container ships do pass through it, but it is the third-largest ocean and it carries two-thirds of the world's oil.

questions.q: What does the chapter mean by 'regionalism'? Give one example of how India's position lets her practise it.
s: States that regionalism is the countries of a region working together for the benefit of everyone in the region, creating peace, stability and shared progress
Gives one example: India's ports serve as gateways for imports and exports, or her central position lets her provide timely humanitarian aid and disaster relief in the region
questions.a: Regionalism is working together with the other countries of the region for everyone's benefit, which brings peace, stability and shared progress. Example: India's central position lets her send timely humanitarian aid and disaster relief (or her ports act as gateways for imports and exports).

questions.q: Tanvi writes: 'India is a vital link between Southeast Asia, West Asia and Africa mainly because her land boundary is over 15,100 km long.' (a) Which feature of India does the chapter actually give for this role? (b) How does that feature make India a link? (c) Name two benefits the chapter says India gains from this position.
s: (a) Identifies the chapter's reason: India's peninsular shape extending deep into the Indian Ocean, with a long coastline of about 11,100 km, not the length of the land boundary
(b) Explains that this location gives India access to important sea routes that connect Southeast Asia, West Asia and Africa

(c) Names two benefits: a key role in trade and regional cooperation; ports that serve as gateways for imports and exports; a central position for giving timely humanitarian aid and disaster relief (any two)
questions.a: Tanvi is wrong. (a) The chapter credits India's peninsular shape reaching deep into the Indian Ocean and her long coastline. (b) This gives her access to important sea routes joining these regions. (c) It lets her play a key role in trade and regional cooperation, her ports act as gateways for imports and exports, and she can give timely humanitarian aid and disaster relief.

questions.q: The chapter widens the idea of a neighbour step by step. (a) What is the 'traditional view' of a neighbour, and through which two kinds of landscape does India's land boundary pass? (b) What makes a country a maritime neighbour, and what has the ocean carried between such neighbours for centuries? (c) The chapter says that only 'from a high-altitude satellite' can we see Iran, Oman, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia as part of India's maritime neighbourhood. Why are these countries not as plainly neighbours as Sri Lanka and the Maldives? (d) Give two of the chapter's Indian Ocean figures that show why this wider sea neighbourhood matters.
s: (a) A neighbour is a country that shares a land boundary; any two of deserts, plains, forests, mountains, marshes and river valleys
(b) A country connected to another by a shared sea or ocean, even without a direct land border; the ocean has carried trade, cultural exchange and historical ties

(c) Sri Lanka and the Maldives are India's immediate neighbours across the waters; these six share no land border and lie farther away across the sea, so only a wide view showing the whole ocean reveals them as connected to India
(d) Any two: half of the world's container ships, one-third of the bulk cargo and two-thirds of the world's oil pass through the Indian Ocean; it connects countries home to around 2.7 billion people
questions.a: (a) The traditional view counts a country that shares a land boundary; the boundary passes through, for example, deserts and mountains. (b) A maritime neighbour is joined by a shared sea or ocean even without a land border; the ocean has carried trade, cultural exchange and historical ties. (c) Sri Lanka and the Maldives are immediate neighbours across the water, while the other six share no land border and lie farther off, so only a view of the whole ocean shows them as linked to India. (d) Half of the world's container ships and two-thirds of its oil pass through the Indian Ocean (also one-third of bulk cargo; 2.7 billion people in the countries it connects).

questions.q: Which of these would NOT be an example of regionalism as the chapter uses the word?
o: India signing a trade deal with a neighbour on terms meant to benefit only India
India sending relief supplies to a neighbour struck by a cyclone
India and other Indian Ocean countries sharing a tsunami warning network
India's ports handling goods that her neighbours import and export
questions.a: India signing a trade deal with a neighbour on terms meant to benefit only India, because regionalism means working together for the benefit of everyone in the region, and trade alone does not make it regionalism.

questions.q: Which of these Indian states lies along India's border with China?
questions.a: Sikkim. The India-China border runs across Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh; Punjab and Gujarat border Pakistan and Tripura borders Bangladesh.

questions.q: Which pair of monks travelled FROM China TO Indian centres of learning?
questions.a: Faxian and Xuanzang, Chinese monks who came to Indian centres of learning; Bodhidharma and Kumarajiva were Indian monks who went to China.

questions.q: True or False: Buddhism reached China from India before Chinese monks such as Faxian and Xuanzang travelled to Indian centres of learning. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: Buddhism reached China around the 1st century CE through trade and pilgrimage routes, and the Chinese monks came a few centuries later
questions.a: True. Buddhism reached China around the 1st century CE via trade and pilgrimage routes; Faxian and Xuanzang travelled to India a few centuries after that.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The balance of trade between India and China is currently much in China's favour.
Reason (R): India's chief exports to China include iron ore, chemicals and cotton yarn.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The balance favours China because China's exports to India are worth about eight times India's exports to China; R only lists what India sends.

questions.q: Give three examples from the chapter that show the cultural links between India and China.
s: Buddhism, which originated in India, reached China around the 1st century CE through trade and pilgrimage routes

Monks travelled both ways: Indian monks such as Bodhidharma, Dharmakshema and Kumarajiva took Buddhist teachings to China, and Chinese monks such as Faxian and Xuanzang came to Indian centres of learning
In the 13th century Hindu merchants built temples in the Chinese port of Quanzhou; pillars at the Kaiyuan temple show Vishnu, Shiva and stories from the Ramayana and the Puranas
questions.a: (1) Buddhism travelled from India to China around the 1st century CE. (2) Indian monks such as Bodhidharma and Kumarajiva carried Buddhist teachings to China, while Chinese monks such as Faxian and Xuanzang studied in India. (3) Hindu merchants built temples in Quanzhou in the 13th century, with carvings of Vishnu, Shiva and Ramayana stories at the Kaiyuan temple.

questions.q:
The social science club of a school in Gangtok, Sikkim, is making a wall poster about the large neighbour that lies beyond the high mountains to the north of the state. Its notes say the border with this neighbour runs through five Indian states and Union Territories; that in 2024-25 India sold it iron ore, chemicals and cotton yarn and bought electronic items and industrial equipment; and that several Indian companies work there. (a) Name the neighbour and the mountain range that separates it from India.
(b) Name any two Indian states or Union Territories, other than Sikkim, along this border.
(c) In whose favour is the balance of trade between the two countries, and by about how much?
(d) The poster has room for one title: 'An Unequal Trade' or 'Linked by Buddhism since the 1st Century CE'. Decide which title the club's own notes give evidence for, using your answer to (c), and say what the poster loses by leaving out the other.
s: (a) China, separated from India by the Himalayas
(b) Any two of Arunachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Ladakh
(c) In China's favour: China's exports to India are worth about eight times India's exports to China

(d) Chooses 'An Unequal Trade', because every item in the club's notes (the border, the 2024-25 goods, Indian companies there) is present-day evidence and the trade figure, China's exports about eight times India's, supports it directly, while the notes hold nothing on Buddhism; the poster loses the deep spiritual and intellectual ties that began when Buddhism reached China around the 1st century CE
questions.a: (a) China; the Himalayas. (b) Any two of Arunachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Ladakh. (c) China's favour; its exports to India are about eight times India's exports to China. (d) 'An Unequal Trade', because the club's notes are all present-day evidence and the eightfold trade gap supports that title directly, while the notes say nothing about Buddhism; leaving out the other title loses the deep spiritual ties that began when Buddhism reached China around the 1st century CE.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with the description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Kaiyuan temple 2. Kumarajiva 3. Guru Padmasambhava 4. Mahendra
Column B: A. Son of Emperor Ashoka who took Buddhism to Sri Lanka  B. Temple in the Chinese port of Quanzhou with pillar carvings of Vishnu and Shiva  C. Indian monk who carried Buddhist teachings to China  D. Introduced the Vajrayana school of Buddhism to Bhutan
questions.a: 1-B, 2-C, 3-D, 4-A: the Kaiyuan temple in Quanzhou has pillar carvings of Vishnu and Shiva, Kumarajiva was an Indian monk who went to China, Guru Padmasambhava brought Vajrayana to Bhutan, and Mahendra took Buddhism to Sri Lanka.

questions.q: According to the chapter, Bangla is a language common to Bangladesh and which Indian state?
questions.a: West Bengal: the chapter says Bangla is common to Bangladesh and India's state of West Bengal.

questions.q: What does an Indian pilgrim need to cross into Pakistan by the Kartarpur Corridor?
o: Only a permit, not a visa
A visa stamped at Dera Baba Nanak
Both a visa and a permit
questions.a: Only a permit: the Kartarpur Corridor is a visa-free crossing, and pilgrims need a permit but no visa.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Sundarban National Park is important for climate resilience.
Reason (R): The Sundarban mangrove forest serves as a barrier to cyclones.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the forest matters for climate resilience because it acts as a barrier to cyclones.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. Ladakh is the only Indian state or Union Territory named on both the chapter's list for the India-Pakistan border and its list for the India-China border.
II. The Katas Raj temple complex, linked to the Mahabharata, is in Balochistan.
III. India's land border with Bangladesh is longer than her border with China.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. The Pakistan list (Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh) and the China list (Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Ladakh) share only Ladakh. Statement II is wrong: the Katas Raj temple complex is in Pakistan's Punjab; it is the Hinglaj Mata Mandir that is in Balochistan.

questions.q: (a) The Kartarpur Corridor was opened in 2019 to mark Guru Nanak's 550th birth anniversary, and the chapter says he spent the last 18 years of his life at Kartarpur. Taking it that he lived to the age of 70, find the year in which he began living at Kartarpur. Show your working. (b) Before the corridor opened, how could Indian devotees see the Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, and what do pilgrims need now instead of a visa?
s: (a) Born 2019 - 550 = 1469; died 1469 + 70 = 1539; began living at Kartarpur 1539 - 18 = 1521
(b) They could only view it from a distance, using binoculars set up near the border at Dera Baba Nanak in Punjab; now they need only a permit
questions.a: (a) 2019 - 550 = 1469 (birth); 1469 + 70 = 1539 (death); 1539 - 18 = 1521, so he began living at Kartarpur in 1521. (b) Devotees could only view the gurdwara from a distance through binoculars at Dera Baba Nanak; with the corridor they need only a permit, not a visa.

questions.q: (a) Name the two river systems from which the transboundary rivers shared by India and Bangladesh originate. (b) Give two ways in which these rivers matter to people in both countries.
s: (a) The Ganga and the Brahmaputra
(b) First way: agriculture, fisheries or transportation
(b) Second way: another of agriculture, fisheries, transportation, or the livelihoods of millions of people
questions.a: (a) The Ganga and the Brahmaputra. (b) Any two of: they support agriculture, fisheries and transportation, and the livelihoods of millions of people in both countries.

questions.q:
Rina's village lies at the edge of the Sundarban National Park in West Bengal. Last year a cyclone struck the coast; villages behind thick mangrove forest suffered much less damage than villages where the forest had been cut. Now a contractor offers to clear 40 hectares of mangroves next to the village for fish ponds, which he says will earn Rs 6 lakh a year, shared equally among 20 families.
(a) In which country does the larger part of this mangrove forest lie, and about what share of it?
(b) Name the famous big cat that lives in this forest.
(c) What do experts predict Bangladesh will face in coming years because of global warming, and how may this affect people?
(d) Should the village council accept the offer? Work out the income per family and weigh it against the chapter's reasons, including who manages the park.
s: (a) Bangladesh, about two-thirds of the forest (the rest is in India)
(b) The Bengal tiger
(c) Rising sea levels and increasingly intense cyclones; many people are likely to lose their homes or see their livelihoods affected

(d) Income is Rs 6,00,000 / 20 = Rs 30,000 a year per family; a justified judgement, for example rejecting the offer because the cyclone report shows the mangroves act as a barrier to cyclones, which will matter more as cyclones grow more intense, and the UNESCO site's protection is coordinated by India and Bangladesh, not decided by one village alone
questions.a: (a) Bangladesh holds about two-thirds of the forest. (b) The Bengal tiger. (c) Rising sea levels and increasingly intense cyclones, so many people may lose their homes or livelihoods. (d) Each family would get Rs 6,00,000 / 20 = Rs 30,000 a year, but the cyclone report shows the mangroves serve as a barrier to cyclones, which will matter more as cyclones grow stronger, and the park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site whose protection the two countries coordinate; so the council should refuse and look for income that keeps the forest.

questions.q: 'India's relationship with Bangladesh is one of the most important in South Asia.' Justify this statement with five different points from the chapter.
s: History: Bangladesh (earlier East Pakistan) was born in 1971 as the outcome of a war between India and Pakistan
Language and culture: Bangla is common to Bangladesh and West Bengal
Border: the land border is even longer than India's border with China and runs along West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
Rivers: shared transboundary river systems from the Ganga and the Brahmaputra support agriculture, fisheries, transport and the livelihoods of millions
Coast and cooperation: a shared coastline and the Sundarban National Park, whose protection the two coordinate, along with strong diplomatic, economic, strategic and cultural cooperation
questions.a: The two share a common history (Bangladesh was born in 1971 from a war between India and Pakistan), a common language (Bangla, also spoken in West Bengal), a land border longer than India's border with China along five states, transboundary rivers of the Ganga and Brahmaputra systems on which millions depend, and a coastline with the jointly protected Sundarbans; on top of this they cooperate diplomatically, economically, strategically and culturally.

questions.q: The people of Bhutan call their country 'Drukyul'. What does the chapter say this name means?
questions.a: Land of the Thunder Dragon.

questions.q: Which agreement provides for the open border and the free movement of people and goods between India and Nepal?
o: The 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship
The agreement that opened the Kartarpur Corridor
questions.a: The 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, which provides for open borders, free movement of people and goods, and cooperation in defence and foreign policy.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column A with its description in Column B.
Column A: 1. Pashupatinatha temple 2. Tala Hydroelectric Project 3. Tiger's nest 4. Gross National Happiness
Column B: A. A Buddhist monastery high above the Paro valley in Bhutan  B. Bhutan's holistic measure of national progress  C. A Hindu pilgrimage site in Kathmandu where Shiva is worshipped as protector of animals  D. Built with India's support and dedicated by the two prime ministers in 2008
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B: the Pashupatinatha temple is in Kathmandu, the Tala project was dedicated in 2008, Tiger's nest overhangs the Paro valley, and Gross National Happiness is Bhutan's measure of progress.

questions.q: True or False: Because thousands of Indians visit the Pashupatinatha temple in Kathmandu every year, the religious and cultural traffic between India and Nepal runs in one direction only, from India to Nepal. Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: pilgrims from both countries regularly visit sacred sites across the border, and festivals such as Dashain, Tihar and Holi are observed with equal enthusiasm in both countries
questions.a: False. Pilgrims from both India and Nepal regularly visit sacred sites across the border, and Dashain, Tihar and Holi are celebrated in both countries.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bhutanese pilgrims frequently visit Buddhist sites in India such as Bodh Gaya, Rajgir and Nalanda.
Reason (R): Bhutan is a small, landlocked Himalayan kingdom lying between India and China.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The pilgrims come because of the shared heritage of Buddhism and the influence of Indian masters such as Guru Padmasambhava, not because Bhutan is landlocked.

questions.q: What is an 'open border'? Give one way in which the India-Nepal open border helps people living near it.
s: An open border is one that people of the two countries can cross without a visa or passport
One way it helps: families on both sides stay connected, or people move easily for education, healthcare, work, trade or religious visits
questions.a: An open border lets people of the two countries cross without a visa or passport. It helps border families stay in touch and lets people move easily for school, healthcare, jobs, trade or pilgrimage.

questions.q: The chapter says the India-Nepal relationship is shaped by 'a shared history, faith, geography, and a commitment to regional harmony'. Choose three of these four and give one piece of evidence from the chapter for each.
s: First chosen idea with matching evidence, e.g. faith: Indian pilgrims visit the Pashupatinatha temple in Kathmandu, and Dashain, Tihar and Holi are celebrated in both countries
Second chosen idea with matching evidence, e.g. geography: a long, open border along Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim allowing centuries of interaction

Third chosen idea with matching evidence, e.g. regional harmony or history: the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship and cooperation in defence and foreign policy; India as Nepal's largest trading partner; working together to keep the open border safe
questions.a: Faith: pilgrims cross to sacred sites such as the Pashupatinatha temple and both celebrate Dashain, Tihar and Holi. Geography: a long open border along five Indian states has allowed centuries of interaction. Regional harmony: the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship, cooperation in defence and foreign policy, and joint care that the open border is not misused.

questions.q:
The chapter asks: 'If borders were drawn only by culture and connections, how would the map look different?' Answer this for Nepal and Bhutan.
(a) What does daily life in many India-Nepal border towns show, according to the chapter?
(b) What is the dragon on Bhutan's emblem and flag said to symbolise, and why does that link Bhutan to India?
(c) What is the 'Tiger's nest' in the Paro valley, and which shared heritage does it reflect?
(d) Bhutan measures its progress by a Gross National Happiness Index rather than only by Gross Domestic Product. Does this difference make Bhutan look more separate from India on a culture-and-connections map? Give a reason.
(e) Give your overall judgement: on such a map, would India, Nepal and Bhutan look more joined or more separate?
s: (a) Close interdependence: vibrant markets and thriving trade
(b) The 'thunderous voice of the Buddha's teachings'; Buddhism grew in India, and Indian masters such as Guru Padmasambhava brought the Vajrayana school to Bhutan
(c) A Buddhist monastery perched high on the mountainside; it reflects the shared heritage of Buddhism

(d) A reasoned view, e.g. it marks Bhutan's own way of measuring progress, but it does not cut the faith, pilgrimage and trade links, so it adds a distinct feature without separating Bhutan from India

(e) Judgement weighing (a) to (d), e.g. more joined: markets and trade across the Nepal border and Buddhism with Bhutan would show one connected zone, with Bhutan's own ideas such as Gross National Happiness as local colour inside it
questions.a: (a) Close interdependence, with vibrant markets and thriving trade. (b) The thunderous voice of the Buddha's teachings; Buddhism came from India, and Guru Padmasambhava brought Vajrayana to Bhutan. (c) A Buddhist monastery high above the Paro valley, reflecting the shared Buddhist heritage. (d) Not much: Gross National Happiness is Bhutan's own measure of progress, but it does not break the faith, pilgrimage and trade ties. (e) More joined: the border towns and the shared Buddhism would make the three look like one connected zone, with Bhutan keeping its own ideas within it.

questions.q: Which of these Indian states shares a border with Myanmar?
questions.a: Manipur. Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram border Myanmar; Tripura and Meghalaya border Bangladesh, and Sikkim borders Nepal, Bhutan and China.

questions.q: What did the Land Border Crossing Agreement of 2018 between India and Myanmar do?
o: It eased cross-border movement for people living in border areas
It opened a visa-free corridor for pilgrims to a gurdwara
It set up a tsunami early warning network
It made Myanmar a member of SAARC
questions.a: It eased cross-border movement for people living in border areas, and so boosted trade, connectivity and people-to-people ties.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The gigantic Buddhas of Bamiyan no longer stand in the Afghan cliffs.
Reason (R): They were destroyed in the 7th century CE, when Islam spread in Afghanistan.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: the Bamiyan Buddhas were destroyed in 2001, long after Islam spread in Afghanistan in the 7th century CE.

questions.q: A student says: 'Movement across the India-Myanmar land border has been restricted in the past couple of years, so the 2018 Land Border Crossing Agreement must have failed from the start.' Which reply fits the chapter?
o: The agreement first eased movement and boosted trade; restrictions came later because of conflicts in the border areas
The agreement never covered people in border areas, only goods carried by sea across the Bay of Bengal
The restrictions came because Myanmar left SAARC, which had made the agreement possible
The restrictions came because the Tio River changed course and the boundary had to be redrawn
questions.a: The agreement first eased movement and boosted trade; the restrictions came later because of conflicts in these areas, so it did not fail from the start.

questions.q: (a) Name the ancient trade route that linked the Ganga plains to Central Asia through Afghanistan. (b) Name one Indian city on this route and one thing, other than goods, that flowed along it.
s: (a) The Uttarapatha
(b) One city (Takshashila, Varanasi or Pataliputra) and one non-goods flow (Buddhism, Hinduism, art, philosophy, religion or ideas)
questions.a: (a) The Uttarapatha. (b) For example Takshashila (or Varanasi, Pataliputra); Buddhism, Hinduism, art and philosophy also flowed along it.

questions.q: Before the 7th century CE, Afghanistan was a thriving centre of Buddhist and Hindu culture. Using the chapter, show three different kinds of Indian influence on early Afghanistan, and give one piece of evidence for each.
s: Trade and ideas: the Uttarapatha linked the Ganga plains to Central Asia via Afghanistan, carrying goods, religion and ideas
Governance: kingdoms such as Kapisha and Zabul mirrored Indian systems of governance
Religion and art: the gigantic Buddhas of Bamiyan stood as symbols of Mahayana Buddhism's reach from India
questions.a: Trade and ideas came along the Uttarapatha; governance is seen in the kingdoms of Kapisha and Zabul, which mirrored Indian systems; religion and art are seen in the Bamiyan Buddhas, symbols of Mahayana Buddhism's reach from India.

questions.q: Afghanistan and Myanmar are both neighbours whose land links with India have been made harder. (a) State what has complicated access in each case, and when. (b) In which case does the difficulty lie in a country between India and the neighbour, and in which case on a border that India and the neighbour still share? (c) Give one other kind of boundary that Myanmar has with India and that landlocked Afghanistan cannot have. (d) Decide which neighbour the chapter shows as more open to India today, and justify your decision using (a) to (c).
s: (a) Afghanistan: the creation of Pakistan in 1947 complicated access; Myanmar: restrictions on free movement across the land border over the past couple of years, on account of conflicts in these areas
(b) Afghanistan: Pakistan now lies between India and Afghanistan; Myanmar: the restrictions are on the shared land border along Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram
(c) A maritime boundary in the Bay of Bengal

(d) Decision with reasons, e.g. Myanmar is more open: it still shares a direct land border and a maritime boundary, the 2018 Land Border Crossing Agreement eased movement and trade, and the recent restrictions are linked to conflicts; Afghanistan has had no direct land border since 1947
questions.a: (a) For Afghanistan, the creation of Pakistan in 1947; for Myanmar, restrictions on free movement across the land border in the past couple of years because of conflicts. (b) Pakistan lies between India and Afghanistan, while the Myanmar restrictions are on a border the two still share. (c) Myanmar also has a maritime boundary with India in the Bay of Bengal. (d) Myanmar is more open: it shares both a land border and a sea boundary, the 2018 agreement eased movement and trade, and its restrictions are recent and tied to conflicts, while Afghanistan has had no direct land border since 1947.

questions.q: Which narrow stretch of sea divides India from Sri Lanka?
questions.a: The Palk Strait, about 32 km wide at the nearest point.

questions.q: A quiz asks students to pick the country that is India's neighbour but is NOT a member of SAARC. Which should they pick?
questions.a: Myanmar. SAARC's members are Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. Buddhism was introduced to Sri Lanka in the 3rd century BCE by Mahendra and Sanghamitra.
II. The Maldives consists of over 1,100 islets.
III. The Maldives is only about 32 km from Minicoy.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. The Maldives is about 130 km from Minicoy; 32 km is the nearest distance between India and Sri Lanka.

questions.q: True or False: Sri Lanka's civil war was mainly between the Tamil majority and the Sinhalese minority. Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the war was mainly between the Sinhalese majority (who speak Sinhala) and the Tamil minority, which has close cultural ties to India
questions.a: False. The war was mainly between the Sinhalese majority and the Tamil minority.

questions.q: The chapter calls India the region's 'trusted first responder'. (a) Name two crises in the Maldives in which India helped quickly. (b) What does 'first responder' mean here?
s: (a) Any two of: the 2004 tsunami, the 2014 water crisis in Male, the COVID-19 pandemic
(b) A country that is among the first to arrive with help when a crisis strikes, because it can respond quickly
questions.a: (a) For example the 2004 tsunami and the 2014 water crisis in Male (or COVID-19). (b) India is among the first to send help when a crisis strikes, because she can respond quickly.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Maldives is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change.
Reason (R): The Maldives is a member of the International Solar Alliance, an Indian initiative.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The Maldives is vulnerable because, as an island nation, a sea-level rise of up to 1 metre could partly submerge many of its islands; its Solar Alliance membership is a response, not the cause.

questions.q:
At a youth meeting in Kathmandu, students from eight South Asian countries plan a joint project to share science and health lessons online. The hosting regional association has eight members: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. A delegate says two of the association's earlier projects stalled, while a separate group of four Indian Ocean countries finished a tsunami-warning project on time.
(a) Name this association and the year it was formed.
(b) What does the association aim to share, according to the chapter?
(c) Using the chapter, explain why the two earlier projects may have stalled.
(d) Should the students run the new project through the association or through a smaller group of willing neighbours? Decide, weighing one advantage of each choice.
s: (a) SAARC, the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, formed in 1985
(b) Resources for development in science, education, health and other areas (to promote mutual interests and sociocultural and economic progress)
(c) Political tensions among some members have often disrupted SAARC's functioning

(d) A justified decision weighing both sides: SAARC brings in all eight countries and is built for exactly this kind of sharing, but a smaller purpose-built group, like the other Indian Ocean groups the chapter mentions, may avoid stalls caused by political tensions
questions.a: (a) SAARC, formed in 1985. (b) It aims to share resources for development in science, education, health and other areas. (c) Political tensions among some members have often disrupted its work. (d) For example: start within SAARC so all eight countries benefit, since sharing science and health is its stated aim, but keep a smaller group of willing neighbours ready, as the chapter notes other Indian Ocean groups exist for specific purposes and tensions can stall SAARC. Either choice earns the mark if both sides are weighed.

questions.q: Kunal says: 'The Maldives is only a scatter of tiny islets far out in the ocean, so it cannot matter much to India.' Give three points from the chapter that show he is wrong.
s: Distance and position: the Maldives is only about 130 km from Minicoy in Lakshadweep, which makes it an important neighbour, especially for trade and security in the Indian Ocean
Working ties: the two nations have built strong ties in defence, trade and disaster relief
Shared future: the Maldives is a member of the International Solar Alliance, an Indian initiative that shares research technology on solar energy, a joint effort towards sustainability
questions.a: Kunal is wrong. The Maldives is only about 130 km from India's Minicoy, so it is an important neighbour for trade and security in the Indian Ocean; the two have built strong ties in defence, trade and disaster relief; and the Maldives is a member of the International Solar Alliance, an Indian initiative sharing solar energy research technology.

questions.q: Indian traders who sailed to Java, Sumatra and Malaya called these places 'Suvarnabhumi'. What does the name mean?
questions.a: The golden land; Indian traders went there in search of gold and other valuable resources.

questions.q:
Match each name or word in Column A with its meaning or origin in Column B.
Column A: 1. Ayutthaya 2. Singapuram 3. Dvaravati 4. Archipelago
Column B: A. That which has gates  B. An extensive group of islands  C. Named after Ayodhya, the birthplace of Rama  D. Lion city
questions.a: 1-C, 2-D, 3-A, 4-B: the Ayutthaya Kingdom was named after Ayodhya, the birthplace of Rama; Singapuram means lion city; Dvaravati means 'that which has gates'; an archipelago is an extensive group of islands.

questions.q: True or False: Islam reached Indonesia from the shores of India, long after Indian kingdoms had begun trading with the islands of Java and Sumatra. Give the verdict and the reason.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: maritime trade between Indian kingdoms and Java and Sumatra dates back over 2,000 years, and the chapter says that later Islam travelled to Indonesia from the shores of India
questions.a: True. Trade between Indian kingdoms and Java and Sumatra began over 2,000 years ago; later, Islam travelled to Indonesia from India's shores.

questions.q: Which piece of evidence best shows that India's link with Thailand is part of Thai public life today, not only in the past?
o: The present king of the Chakri dynasty is named Rama X
The Dvaravati culture flourished from the 6th to the 11th century CE
Indian traders and scholars sailed there as early as the 3rd century BCE
The Ayutthaya Kingdom, named after Ayodhya, was founded in 1351
questions.a: The present king of the Chakri dynasty is named Rama X: all the dynasty's monarchs are named after Rama, which shows the link continuing today; the other three are about the past.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Indonesia is one of the most earthquake-prone countries in the world.
Reason (R): Indonesian islands lie in a region that experiences frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: Indonesia is earthquake-prone because its islands lie in a region of frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The name 'Singapore' comes from 'Singapuram', meaning 'lion city'.
Reason (R): Singapore became a separate nation in 1965.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The name comes from an ancient kingdom called Singapuram, centuries before Singapore became a nation in 1965.

questions.q:
A Class 7 group visits an exhibition on Indonesia in New Delhi. The first stall shows a rupiah banknote printed with a large bird, the national symbol. The second shows a model of a huge stone monument built on five enormous platforms and holding over 500 statues of the Buddha. The third shows a map of a country made of several large islands and more than 17,000 smaller ones. The fourth plays a video of Indonesian actors performing a famous Indian epic.
(a) Name the bird on the rupiah and the god whose vahana it is.
(b) Name the monument in the second stall and the sacred design its shape copies.
(c) Which word describes a country made of a large group of islands, like the one on the map?
(d) Which Indian epic does the chapter show Indonesian actors performing?
s: (a) Garuda, the vahana of Vishnu
(b) The Borobudur Stupa; its design replicates a mandala
(c) An archipelago
(d) The Ramayana
questions.a: (a) Garuda, the vahana of Vishnu. (b) The Borobudur Stupa, whose design replicates a mandala. (c) An archipelago. (d) The Ramayana.

questions.q: A travel writer claims: 'Indian influence reached Southeast Asia only through Hinduism.' Evaluate this claim using evidence from Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, and give your verdict.
s: Thailand: Theravada Buddhism is widely practised, alongside Hindu deities and epic stories in royal ceremonies, dance and literature
Malaysia: around the 4th century CE the region adopted a script based on India's Brahmi script, and Indian workers migrated there in the 19th and 20th centuries
Singapore: Tamil is one of its four official languages, Buddhism is now its most widely practised religion, and about 9 per cent of residents are of Indian origin
Indonesia: the Borobudur Stupa is a Buddhist monument, Nalanda collaborated with the Muara Jambi temple complex, and Islam later travelled to Indonesia from India's shores

Verdict: the claim is wrong; Hinduism was one channel (Ayutthaya, Garuda on the rupiah, Ramayana performances), but Buddhism, script, language, trade, migration and even Islam also carried Indian influence
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Thailand widely practises Theravada Buddhism; Malaysia adopted a Brahmi-based script and received Indian migrant workers; Singapore has Tamil as an official language and about 9 per cent Indian-origin residents; Indonesia has the Buddhist Borobudur Stupa, the Nalanda-Muara Jambi link, and Islam that came from India's shores. Hinduism mattered (Ayutthaya, Garuda, the Ramayana), but it was only one of many channels.

questions.q: The Mahabharata mentions a people under the name 'Parasika'. Who were they?
questions.a: The Persians: Indian texts such as the Mahabharata mention Persians under the name Parasika.

questions.q: At a Harappan site in Gujarat, archaeologists find a copper ingot dated to the 3rd millennium BCE. A student says it most likely came from Iran, because India and Iran have shared close ties since the Bronze Age. Which reply fits the chapter best?
o: Oman is the likelier source: the chapter calls Oman rich in copper and links Harappan traders to its ingots, but names no copper trade with Iran.
Iran is right: its Bronze Age ties with India make it the likeliest source of Harappan copper.
Afghanistan is the likelier source: the Uttarapatha carried goods from Central Asia to the Ganga plains.
Iran is right: its ports were within easy reach of India's west coast, and Gujarat lies on that coast.
questions.a: Oman is the likelier source. The chapter says Oman is rich in copper and that Harappan traders are thought to have brought copper ingots from there; its account of India-Iran ties speaks of land and sea routes, language and literature, but not of copper.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Oman shares a land boundary with India.
Reason (R): Oman is India's closest defence partner in the Gulf.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Oman shares maritime boundaries with India, not a land boundary; and Oman is India's closest defence partner in the Gulf, being the first in the region where India holds joint military exercises with all three armed forces.

questions.q:
A Class 7 group is making five cards for a display called 'India and Iran: links old and new'. Use the chapter to complete each card in one step.
(a) Card 1: Old court records of the Mughals in India are full of Persian. Explain why.
(b) Card 2: Name the community of India that the chapter calls a living link with ancient Persian culture.
(c) Card 3: Name the port in Iran that India is helping to develop.
(d) Card 4: India and Afghanistan no longer share a direct land border. Say what this port gives India.
(e) Card 5: Name the three fields in which, the chapter says, India and Iran have cooperated in modern times.
s: (a) Persian was used as the court language in India by the Mughals and other rulers
(b) The Parsis of India
(c) Chabahar Port (the Shahid Beheshti Port at Chabahar)
(d) Better access to Afghanistan and Central Asia
(e) Trade, energy and transport
questions.a: (a) Persian was the court language of the Mughals and other rulers in India. (b) The Parsis. (c) Chabahar Port. (d) Better access to Afghanistan and Central Asia. (e) Trade, energy and transport.

questions.q:
Ravi lives in Muscat. His great-grandfather was a merchant from Kutch in north-western India who settled in Oman. Ravi is writing a letter to a newspaper in India whose readers believe that only countries sharing a land border with India really matter to her. His teacher shows him a map: Oman lies on the south-eastern coast of the Arabian Peninsula, facing India across the Arabian Sea.
(a) What kind of boundary does Oman share with India, and why does that still make Oman India's neighbour?
(b) Ravi's family story is an example of which link described in the chapter? Give the chapter's figure that shows how large this link is.
(c) Name the two waters at whose meeting point Oman lies, and the role the chapter gives Oman in India's engagement with the Gulf region.
(d) The letter has room for only one argument: P, 'Indian-origin families settled in Oman share a living people-to-people bond with India', or Q, 'Oman is India's closest defence partner in the Gulf and works with India on Indian Ocean maritime security'. Which better answers these readers? Decide, and say what the letter loses by leaving out the other.
s: (a) Oman shares maritime boundaries with India; a maritime neighbour is a country connected to another by a shared sea or ocean, even without a direct land border
(b) Merchant communities from north-western parts of India settled in Oman over the past few centuries; over 10% of Oman's population is of Indian origin
(c) The Persian Gulf and the Arabian Sea; Oman is a key partner in India's engagement with the Gulf region, plays an important role in regional forums and holds significant strategic importance

(d) A justified decision weighing both: for example Q, because readers who value land borders are answered best by showing Oman is a security partner across the sea (first in the region for joint exercises with all three armed forces), though the letter then loses the living people-to-people bond of the Indian-origin community shown by P (or the reverse, defended with care)
questions.a: (a) Maritime boundaries; a maritime neighbour is joined by a shared sea even without a land border. (b) The settlement of merchant communities from north-western India in Oman over the past few centuries; over 10% of Oman's people are of Indian origin. (c) The Persian Gulf and the Arabian Sea; Oman is a key partner in India's engagement with the Gulf, active in regional forums and strategically important. (d) For example Q: it shows these readers that a sea neighbour can be India's closest defence partner in the Gulf, the first in the region for joint exercises with all three armed forces; but the letter loses P's evidence of a living bond between the two peoples.

questions.q: Meena says: 'In ancient times India and Iran could be in contact only over land, along the routes that later became the Silk Route.' Is she right, partly right or wrong? Give reasons from the chapter.
s: Accepts the true part: trade and cultural exchange took place early through land routes passing through present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan, which gradually became part of the Silk Route
Points out the missing part: sea routes were also used, since Iran's ports were within easy reach of India's west coast
Verdict: partly right, because land routes were one way but not the only way
questions.a: Partly right. Land routes through present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan did carry early contact and became part of the Silk Route, but sea routes were also used because Iran's ports were within easy reach of India's west coast.

questions.q: India shares no land border with Iran or Oman. Evaluate the statement 'Being neighbours is not just about geography' by showing, in five points from the chapter, that both countries are still close neighbours of India. Each point must use evidence about both Iran and Oman.
s: Sea: Oman shares maritime boundaries with India; Iran's ports were within easy reach of India's west coast
Ancient contact: India and Iran have had ties since the Bronze Age; India-Oman contact goes back over 5,000 years to the Harappan copper trade
Culture and language: the Avesta has parallels with the Rigveda and Persian was a Mughal court language; Oman has a Shiva temple, the Motishwar Mandir, in Muscat
People: the Parsis of India are a living link with ancient Persian culture; over 10 per cent of Oman's population is of Indian origin
Today: India is developing Iran's Chabahar Port for access to Afghanistan and Central Asia; Oman is India's closest defence partner in the Gulf, so the statement is supported
questions.a: The statement holds. Both are joined to India by the sea (Oman's maritime boundary, Iran's nearby ports); both have very old contact (Bronze Age links with Iran, 5,000-year-old copper trade with Oman); both share culture (Avesta and Rigveda, Persian at Mughal courts; the Motishwar Mandir in Muscat); both are tied by people (the Parsis; Indians as over 10 per cent of Oman's people); and both are partners today (Chabahar Port; Oman as India's closest Gulf defence partner).

questions.q: (a) Name the object from Oman, dated to the 3rd millennium BCE, that the chapter links with Harappan traders, and name the Shiva temple in Muscat that the Hindu community was allowed to build in the early 20th century. (b) Using these two, explain why India-Oman contact can be called both very old and still continuing.
s: (a) A copper ingot from Oman; the Motishwar Mandir

(b) The ingot shows contact over 5,000 years ago, when Harappan traders are thought to have brought Omani copper to the Indus-Sarasvati cities; the temple shows an Indian community still living and worshipping in Oman thousands of years later, so the contact is very old and has continued
questions.a: (a) A copper ingot from Oman and the Motishwar Mandir. (b) The ingot points to contact in Harappan times, over 5,000 years ago; the temple, allowed in the early 20th century, shows Indians still settled in Oman in recent times. So the contact is very old and has carried on.
